name: Volcano Suns
label: Homestead
lede: Mission of Burma's drummer walked off the stage of the loudest band in Boston and started another one, then went through four guitarists and three bassists and ended up recorded by Steve Albini.

eras.title: After the earplugs
eras.text: Mission of Burma ends in 1983 because its guitarist can't stand the volume. Its drummer is the one who wants to keep playing loud.

years.src: Wikipedia: Mission of Burma · Wikipedia: Volcano Suns
years.p: Miller wore rifle-range earmuffs over foam earplugs on the farewell tour. Drummer Peter Prescott was the one who wasn't done.
years.xp:
Mission of Burma broke up in 1983 because of Miller's worsening tinnitus, blamed on the band's live volume, according to Wikipedia. The farewell tour was captured on The Horrible Truth About Burma, released in 1985.

Prescott had shared singing and songwriting with Miller and Clint Conley, and had also drummed in a band called the Molls. What he did next was start a band where he drummed and did the singing.

years.cap: Peter Prescott at the Rathskeller, Boston
years.src: Wikipedia: Volcano Suns · The Village Voice · Slant · PopMatters
years.h: Prescott starts Volcano Suns with Gary Waleik and Steve Michener
years.p: Spring 1984, Boston. Prescott plays drums and sings; Waleik plays guitar (and sitar), Michener plays bass.
years.xp:
Wikipedia dates the band's founding to Spring 1984 and calls Prescott the only founding member to stay until the 1991 breakup. Prescott has said he was "looking around for people" and that Homestead's Gerard Cosloy was one of the first people he sent Suns material to, per the Village Voice.

The formula was straight rock songs where the guitars blare rather than jangle, as Slant put it, minus the tape-loop manipulation of his old band, according to PopMatters.

eras.title: Two guys out to fool around
eras.text: The first real lineup records two albums for a combined $1,800 and gets a B+ from Christgau and a top-ten nod in Philadelphia. Two-thirds of the band would have preferred not to be noticed.

years.src: Wikipedia: Volcano Suns · Wikipedia: Big Dipper
years.h: Waleik and Michener leave to found [[Big Dipper|0ec95aa0-d79b-4d02-946c-bf8867f7e054]]; Weigand and Williams arrive
years.p: Jeff Weigand takes bass, Jon Williams takes guitar, and this trio makes both Homestead albums.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says Waleik and Michener left after about 16 months. Big Dipper's Wikipedia page says the band was formed by former members of Volcano Suns and the Embarrassment, and that Bill Goffrier was recruited after he saw a Volcano Suns show in mid-1985.

Big Dipper also landed on Homestead, with the Boo-Boo EP and Heavens in 1987.

years.src: Indy Week · Slant · Robert Christgau · Consequence · Wikipedia: The Bright Orange Years
years.h: The Bright Orange Years: $800 and a song called "Jak"
years.p: Homestead released the debut, engineered by Lou Giordano, with "Jak" opening the record.
years.xp:
Indy Week reports the album was recorded for $800. Slant called "Jak" "clearly one of the best blastoffs of the '80s." Christgau gave the record a B+, saying the first side had everything an insatiable Burma or Hüsker Dü fan could ask for except Richard Harte's production.

Indy Week also says Weigand and Williams treated the band as a chance to fool around and steered away from getting ahead, while Prescott, who had done this once already, was willing to work the promotion. Weigand told Indy Week's David Klein about being left in a room with Bruce Springsteen's guitar and told not to touch it; he picked up the Telecaster, plucked it and broke the strings, according to Consequence.

years.src: Indy Week · Wikipedia: All-Night Lotus Party · Trouser Press · Exclaim!
years.p: Eleven songs open with "White Elephant" and close with "Ride the Cog"; the Washington Post called the opener a post-punk romp, clamorous but tightly structured.
years.xp:
Indy Week gives the recording cost as $1,000. The New York Times said the band was defining its own punk-pop-metal turf, and the Philadelphia Inquirer ranked the record among 1986's ten best, per Wikipedia. Trouser Press hears less melody than on the debut, because Prescott wrote less of it, and points to "Cans" and "Dot on the Map".

The same year, Homestead put out a "Sea Cruise" b/w "Greasy Spine" seven-inch, both later bonus tracks on the Merge reissue.

eras.title: New bassist, a trumpet, a sitar
eras.text: Two-thirds of the band quits at once and Prescott rebuilds around a bassist who will outlast him. The records get stranger and the guest list longer.

years.src: Trouser Press · Wikipedia: Mission of Burma · Indy Week
years.h: Weigand and Williams out; Bob Weston and Chuck Hahn in
years.p: Trouser Press dates the exit to March 1987. Weston takes bass, Hahn takes guitar, and Prescott is the last original left.
years.xp:
Weston stayed to the end, engineered later reissues, and joined Mission of Burma in 2002, replacing Martin Swope. He is also a member of Shellac, and Steve Albini recorded the Suns' last album.

In 2009 Weigand was reported by Indy Week to be delivering mail in Vermont after twelve years chasing a psychology doctorate in Belgium; Williams lived in northern Vermont.

years.src: Wikipedia: Volcano Suns · Trouser Press · Robert Christgau
years.h: Bumper Crop on Homestead, with Roger Miller on piano
years.p: Miller, Prescott's old bandmate, plays piano, and Gary Waleik returns on sitar.
years.xp: Trouser Press says Prescott took back the songwriting and returned to the structures of the debut. Christgau graded it B-, said it was a little too dirgy-anthemic to review, and noted that the press release was worth quoting.

years.h: The trio backs Dredd Foole as the Din
years.p: Eat My Dust Cleanse My Soul credits Prescott as Din Wanna, Weigand as Bonus "The Bone Man" McGinty and Williams as Webb Finga.
years.xp: Wikipedia lists the record, on Homestead, as the second lineup backing vocalist Dredd Foole under stage names. The Din returned in 1988 with Take Off Your Skin on PVC.

years.src: Wikipedia: Farced · Wikipedia: Volcano Suns · Robert Christgau · Trouser Press
years.h: Greg Ginn's SST puts out Farced, with trumpet, sitar and cello
years.p: Robert Christgau, giving the record a B+, on the half of Mission of Burma that hadn't turned to chamber music.
years.xp: The band moved to [[Greg Ginn|4f35de64-27ab-4426-95fd-8d454cda4e48]]'s SST for its fourth release, per Wikipedia. Weston plays trumpet, Chris George sitar, Tricia Matthews violin and cello, and Nick Maldonado a sampler; Sean Slade co-produced at Fort Apache South. Trouser Press says too many songs dissolve into a cacophonous blur, while Wikipedia notes Spin put it on a list of 80 excellent records of the 80s.

eras.title: Everybody sings
eras.text: With David Kleiler on guitar, the band goes democratic, then spends its last record with Steve Albini behind the desk. The end arrives without a fight.

years.src: Wikipedia: Thing of Beauty (album) · Trouser Press · Wikipedia: Farced
years.h: Thing of Beauty: a double album on SST, and a Brian Eno cover
years.p: David Kleiler settles in on guitar, and he and Weston share lead vocals with Prescott.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says the band swapped instruments during recording and calls it a shift toward democratic songwriting. Trouser Press counts nineteen originals plus "Needles in the Camel's Eye". Wikipedia's tracklist runs to seventeen, with two on CD and cassette only.

Wikipedia dates Kleiler's arrival to 1989, though the Farced credits already list him on guitar.

years.src: Wikipedia: Volcano Suns · Wikipedia: Career in Rock
years.h: "Blue Rib" b/w "Openings" and an MC5 cover on Duck and Cover
years.p: Quarterstick issues the single; SST's Duck and Cover compilation carries a Suns version of the MC5's "Kick Out the Jams".
years.xp: Wikipedia lists both. "Blue Rib" reappears on Career in Rock the next year.

years.src: Wikipedia: Career in Rock · Do You Compute · Slant
years.h: Career in Rock: Albini records the last one for Quarterstick
years.p: Steve Albini recorded the trio of Prescott, Bob Weston and David Kleiler, and one blogger called it some of Albini's best work.
years.xp: Quarterstick was the Chicago label tied to Touch and Go, which is why some reviews say Touch and Go. A reviewer at Do You Compute praised Prescott's booming drums, Weston's chunky bass and Kleiler's seventh chords, plus anthemic team vocals. The Boston Herald said the group never failed to make an aggressive, tuneful and loud punk rush.

years.src: Wikipedia: Volcano Suns · Wikipedia: Career in Rock
years.p: Wikipedia says the band split in 1991; its Career in Rock article has the breakup announced before a Chicago show in 1992.
years.xp:
The sources disagree by about a year. The band's Wikipedia page gives 1991; the album page gives 1992 and a Chicago show.

Weston and Albini went on to Shellac; Prescott started Kustomized and, later, went back to Burma.

eras.title: Second lives, and CDs at last
eras.text: Prescott goes back to the guitar and to Burma, the Suns reappear for a handful of shows, and Merge finally puts the first two albums on CD.

years.src: Wikipedia: Thing of Beauty (album) · Wikipedia: Volcano Suns
years.p: His next band. Wikipedia says the guitar he picked up during Thing of Beauty became the focus.
years.xp: Wikipedia's Thing of Beauty page links Prescott's guitar work on the record to his later band Kustomized.

years.h: Mission of Burma reunites, with Bob Weston for Martin Swope
years.p: Two shows turn into a full comeback after the tickets sell out quickly.
years.xp: Wikipedia's Mission of Burma article gives 2002 for the reunion; PopMatters dates Prescott's return to Burma to 2004.

years.src: Indy Week · The Village Voice · Wikipedia: Volcano Suns
years.h: The Suns play a few reunion shows
years.p: The 1989 trio of Prescott, Weston and Kleiler is back, and Yo La Tengo's Ira Kaplan pushed for it.
years.xp: Indy Week names Kaplan as the spark; the Village Voice mentions a Yo La Tengo Hanukkah performance among the sporadic shows.

years.cap: Merge's 2009 reissue of The Bright Orange Years
years.src: Exclaim! · The Big Takeover · Consequence · Indy Week
years.h: Merge reissues the first two albums on CD
years.p: Mac McCaughan's label puts out The Bright Orange Years and All-Night Lotus Party, remastered by Weston, with eleven bonus tracks each.
years.xp:
Exclaim reported the reissues on January 27, 2009 and said they nearly double the length of the originals, with WERS radio sessions, alternate versions and a reworked hidden track retitled "superhappyfunmysterybonustrack2009". Big Takeover notes covers of Prince's "1999" and Leonard Nimoy's "The Ballad of Bilbo Baggins".

Consequence says the band members supervised the reissues closely; Indy Week says the original liner notes were farcical, including a line about the world's greatest motorcycle daredevils.

years.h: Old Pain(t) puts out a City Gardens show from summer 1986
years.p: Merge releases a live album with the Weigand and Williams trio recorded at the New Jersey club.
years.xp: Wikipedia dates the release to July 2014 and the recording to summer 1986 at City Gardens in New Jersey.
